THE YMCAs oF ouéEsBec 


THE TIES THAT BIND 


The future looks bright for Québec YMCAs. In 2007, we 
launched and completed some outstanding projects that have 
already had an impact on our communities. 


We are pleased to have submitted a position paper to the 
Consultation Commission on Accommodation Practices 
Related to Cultural Differences. It once again confirmed our 
values of “accessibility”, wish for dialogue, as well as our role as a community 
crossroads where everyone can discover themselves, meet each other and rec- 
oncile their differences. You only need to visit the Y to see that these values are 
part of everyday life. 


If self-respect and respect for others are principles that guide our actions, the 
family was clearly a core concern for us this year. Among other things, we 
launched a family membership plan and adopted a program of activities cus- 
tomized for parents and their children. The project required major investments, 
considerable effort on the part of a number of employees and volunteers in all our 
departments, and was favourably received by families in our communities. 


The YMCA also has good news on the development front: the plan to build a 
Community Aquatics and Sports Complex in Cartierville has been approved. In 
2010, Ahuntsic-Cartierville residents will have access to the new facilities that will 
include: a pool, gym, raised jogging track, physical fitness centre, daycare, and 
several multipurpose rooms. 


We can also talk about a resurgence of the YMCA in Québec City. With the sup- 
port of highly dedicated volunteers and the cooperation of new partners, we have 
expanded the scope of the Compensatory Work Program and of the Alternative 
Suspension program to Québec City. This increased presence in the old capital 
bodes well for the future. 


The fact that our influence now extends beyond the Greater Montreal area has led 
us to adopt a new name: The YMCAs of Québec. The new name reflects our actu- 
al reach and will support our development strategy. 


Finally, we can hardly keep quiet about the moving 20* anniversary of the Peace 
Medal Awards, an event that honours peacemakers and justice-seekers around 
the world. The YMCA gave special recognition to two child soldiers who were res- 
cued from Sierra Leone. 


Many thanks to all our staff, volunteers, donors and participants. Through their 
beliefs and dedication, the YMCA can strengthen its ties with communities every 


day. 


Caroline Sauriol Stéphane Vaillancourt 
Chair of the Board of Directors President and Chief Executive Officer

THE YMCA FouNDATION 


THE TIES THAT BIND 


This past year was very fruitful, bringing new projects and 
opportunities, along with time to reflect on the role of the 
Foundation and to plan our future. 


Our strategic discussions led us to review our mission state- 
ment and clarify some ambitious strategic objectives. Starting 
this year, we will be intensifying our efforts to represent and 
promote the YMCA to better support our programs and philanthropic activities. 
We have also returned to a structure of working committees and reaffirmed the 
role and responsibilities of each board member. 


Strengthening our ties with the Québec business community will be a major focus. 
Many companies are already engaged with the YMCA as corporate citizens 
through their donation or sponsorship programs. Our task will be to enhance the 
YMCA’s image with this clientele by clearly positioning itself as a leading organi- 
zation dedicated to the well-being of children and youth. The YMCA and its 
Foundation must be seen and recognized as charitable partners of choice for 
companies who want to have a positive impact in their community. 


A wonderful example of such a partnership is the “Adopt-a-School” project 
described later in this report. Projects like this have the potential to develop on a 
larger scale and to involve even more corporate partners. 


The Foundation has a significant but achievable amount of work to do. With 
increased funding and increased notoriety, the YMCA will be better able to 
strengthen our communities through new initiatives, programs and high-quality 
infrastructures. The overall goal is to increase the number of people who benefit 
from our actions and reinforce the ties that unite us all. 


We would like to conclude by thanking Claude A. Garcia who has played a lead- 
ing role on the Foundation’s Board: of Directors for the past 10 years. Mr. Garcia 
had a strong influence on the Y right from the beginning. In 1999, he started out as 
the chairman of the Downtown YMCA’s Revitalization Campaign, a project he 
undertook with great enthusiasm. The campaign raised $11 million, which was 
used to finance a community centre open to all in the heart of the city. He became 
chairman of the board of directors the following year. Throughout his mandate, 
Mr. Garcia was deeply committed, highly energetic and extremely generous. He 
resigned from the position on May 15, 2007. We wish him every success in his 
future endeavors. 


Mize ey. 


Michael Goldboom Michael Novak 


Chair of the Board of Directors President

campers were soaking in the rain. 
Suddenly, a thunderstorm struck with 
high winds. Chloé had already been 
paddling for hours. She was running 
out of energy and feeling discour- 
aged. She was at the end of her rope. 


The girl turned around and saw the 
kind look on Bex’s face. Bex, her 
had been 
watching her for some time and could

that no matter what happened, she 
could count on Bex. 


The two girls met on that camping 
expedition. Today they laugh about 
the tough time that has become one of 
the best memories of their lives.

trip, and really be yourself, 
without any pretenses

Claude D. Chomski, Member 
Yaffa Gruia, Personal trainer 


wo and a half years ago, Claude 

Chomski was a man in relatively 
good shape—more or less. He had 
never shown any great skill or liking for 
sports, other than the recent exception 
of walking. “Body mechanics are still a 
mystery to me. For as long as | can 
remember, | was always dead last in 
my gym class,” he said. 


nn 
ZUU i 


& 
ae 


At an age when other people retire, 
Claude felt the need to become active, 
to “invest in my physical and mental 
health.” Still, he wasn't keen on doing 
it alone and thought that some guid- 
ance would help. The YMCA teamed 
him up with Yaffa. 


Yaffa is a personal trainer who has 
been with the Y for close to 15 years. 
She advises and guides Westmount 
YMCA members in their efforts to 
maintain or improve their physical 
shape. She is in great shape, full of 
energy, positive and outgoing—in 
short, a real pro. 


“When the Y assigns me someone, | 
form a team with that person. | share in 
his or her success or failure. Although 
it was a challenge, | believe that ‘we’ 
succeeded in making great progress,” 
said Yaffa. 


Little by little, Claude improved his 
cardio health and muscle strength. 
“| discovered muscles | never even 
knew existed,” he added. The two 
of them got to know and appreciate 
each other. Then again, that's to be 
expected, since they have spent two 
hours a week together for the past 

two years now. 


THAT BIND 


THE 


In 2007, Claude had already completed 
multiple half-marathon walks, the last 
in 3 hours and 8 minutes. He uses his 
car less and less because he walks 
most of the time. Claude convinced his 
wife to come to the Y and has even 
become the trainer for a small walking 
group. Claude has changed his self- 
image and his quality of life just keeps 
getting better. 


Yaffa believes that progress is all a 
matter of perspective. You have to 
respect each person's pace. “If you 
could only do one sit-up before, but 
then you can manage to do two, 
that's a 100% improvement!” she 
concluded.

YMCA KANAWANA 
MAKING PROGRESS... 


The development of Quebec’s first “green” camp is moving forward. YMCA 
Kanawana is reducing its environmental impact and becoming a model for all. 


The YMCA Kanawana Development Project represents an investment of close to 
$5 million in total. Last spring, two new environmentally friendly sanitary 
facilities were built on the site and made ready for the first campers of the 
year. Controlled water flow in the taps and showers, a wastewater heat recov- 
ery system, and composting toilets help reduce water consumption by 50%. 


The sanitary complex also has a new artesian well, a wastewater treatment and 
distribution system, as well as an artificial marsh. These new facilities were put 
to the test all summer long by the young campers who also benefited from an environmental education pro- 
gram set up by the YMCA where they learned the basics of sustainable development. Our goal is that they 
will transfer their newly acquired knowledge to their everyday lives. 


In a subsequent phase, the fundraising campaign will enable the YMCA to build three-season facilities for 
schools and community groups that will visit Kanawana in the spring and fall. 


ORGANIC COMMUNITY GARDEN AND COMPOSTING 

In addition, Camp YMCA Kanawana developed an educational program on organic gardening in cooperation 
with the Pointe-Saint-Charles YMCA. Seniors and youth were matched up for seeding and planting, as well 
as for composting activities overseen by an organic vegetable garden landscaper. 


A PIECE OF PARADISE FOR EVERYONE 

Knowing that the camp plays a positive role in the lives of young people, the YMCA wanted to make the 
Kanawana experience accessible to a wider clientele. In partnership with its nine centres and various com- 
munity organizations, 19% of Kanawana’s campers—a measurable increase year after year—will receive 
financial assistance from now on. 


THE TIES THAT BIND 


After all, every kid deserves a little piece of paradise...

ADOPT-A-SCHOOL PROJECT 
AN INNOVATIVE FORMULA FOR 
PROMOTING EQUAL OPPORTUNITIES 


When a leading corporate citizen and charity organization come together... 
miracles can happen. 


Born of the desire of Desjardins Assets Management to encourage success at school and by 
the concrete initiatives of the Guy-Favreau YMCA, “Adopt-a-School” is aimed at primary 
schools in underprivileged areas and, more specifically, their students. The goal is to sup- 
port equal opportunities for all while motivating school retention in various ways. 


There is a tremendous need in some schools for after-school and enrichment programs, out- 


ings, and computer and sports equipment. Three elementary schools in Montreal's Centre-South area 
(Champlain, Marguerite-Bourgeoys and Jean-Baptiste-Meilleur) were the first to benefit from Desjardins 
Assets Management's generosity. Their financial contribution to the project, along with that of their part- 
ners, amounts to $800,000 over five years. 


Already, a computer room with 30 workstations has been set 

up, camperships have been provided to children who rarely 

have a chance to leave the city, and young students have 

enjoyed theatre subscriptions, a trip to Québec City, a plant- 13 
ing program, and workshops on the environment and recy- 

cling. 


Close to 2,000 students have been reached through these 
various measures. 


Having surpassed expectation in its success, “Adopt-a- 
School” has become an excellent model for social commit- 
ment that will surely be extended to other schools. All cor- 


a 
porations and organizations that are looking to support the 2 
education of our youth are encouraged to sign up! co

ENDOWMENT FUND 
IDEAS AND PROJECTS THAT COME FROM THE HEART 


Philanthropy, charity, giving, volunteer work, sponsorship, assistance, relief work...so many words 
express the generosity of individuals who believe in the YMCA’s mission and support it through the 
Endowment Fund. 


Their generosity enables the nine YMCA centres and Camp YMCA Kanawana to continue offering 
essential community programs and to develop new ones. 


In January 2007, the market value of the Endowment Fund was $4.98 million. According to the 
revenue allocation method, 4% of the Fund is used for community programs during the year. As a 
result, $199,200 was distributed to carry out the YMCA’s mission in 2007. 


A portion of the revenues (i.e., $101,592) supports programs chosen by donors, such as homework help at 
the Pointe-Saint-Charles YMCA and the Development Project for YMCA Kanawana. A sum of $88,521 was allo- 
cated to projects selected by a committee composed of volunteers on the Foundation’s Board of Directors 
and YMCA representatives.

THE YMCAs oF aouéBeEc 


HIGHLIGHTS 2007 


PHILANTHROPY AND VOLUNTEERISM 


Every day, people discover who we are and what we do. Our actions are recog- 
nized, appreciated and encouraged. At its origin, philanthropy means “the love of 
humankind”: it represents the spirit of giving of oneself for the benefit of others. As 
a result, an invisible tie is formed between a troubled student and a volunteer school 
mentor, an immigrant and a welcome staff, an older member and his or her trainer, 
etc. The Y facilitates chain reactions, removes barriers, opens hearts, and gener- 
ates ideas and projects. Everyone benefits from the strong spirit of giving at the Y. 


People have their own way of lighting up their world, city and community through 
their generosity. 


In 2007, the YMCA Community Support Campaign, organized in each of our centres, 
raised close to $310,000, which is double the amount raised five years ago. 


The generosity of members and donors, both individual and corporate, means that 
community programs are accessible to the largest number of people possible. In 
2007, 5,613 people received $676,000 in financial assistance from the YMCA to have the opportunity to partici- 
pate in our programs. 


Year after year, the YMCA can count on the support of more than 1,300 volunteers who work in all areas of activ- 
ity. Whether they are motivated by compassion, ideas, or a vision, our volunteers support us in our actions with 
energy and dedication that enriches the lives of thousands of people. 


This year’s work by volunteers on the board of directors was outstanding, especially the Governance Commit- 
tee, which laid the foundations for a plan that will enable the YMCA to renew members’ interest in our activities. 


The YMCA also confirmed its intention to improve support for volunteers by creating a new position. The new 
recruit will report to the Human Resources Department and be in charge of creating a volunteer development plan. © 


THE TIES THAT BIND 


PHYSICAL ACTIVITIES 


As part of the new family membership plan, new physical fitness and childhood development 
programs were introduced in various YMCA centres. This resulted in much higher attendance in our 
yoga, dance, physical ‘activity and aqua mom & baby classes by parents, teens, babies and 
preschoolers. 


The West Island, Westmount, Du Parc and Notre-Dame-de-Grace YMCAs were among the first to 
offer the family membership. The four centres considerably exceeded their membership objectives. 


16 The same thing happened in water sports/aqua-fitness. We saw strong participation in all programs. 
We also introduced continuous registration, a measure that encourages family participation and promotes 
more efficient learning. 


Our training program for instructors and “FIT” trainers was once again highly successful. The YMCA clearly 
remains a leader in physical activity training. 


COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT 


No less than 35 youth and 20 parents learned to cook healthy and delicious meals from various culi- 
nary traditions on a limited budget. The Notre-Dame-de-Grace YMCA offered this activity. 


Some thirty families participated in the Saint-Laurent YMCA interactive workshops, which are aimed 
at strengthening the family’s educational role with a view towards overall childhood development. 


From now on, students from three high schools in the Pointe-de-l‘ile school board and students from 
Joliette and Québec City will have an alternative if they're suspended from school. The program, 
which is coordinated by the Du Parc YMCA, now includes new locations in addition to the five existing ones. 
They offer workshops that encourage youth to think about going back to school and staying there. 


More than 60 people regularly attend the Pointe-Saint-Charles YMCA Seniors’ Days. Having board games, dis- 
cussion groups, physical therapy, presentations on urban safety, cultural outings, tai chi and other activities 
helps seniors avoid isolation and age more healthily. 


CHILD DEVELOPMENT 


The “Playing to Learn” educational approach in Canadian YMCAs is currently being implemented in 
Montreal YMCAs that have programs for preschoolers. The approach promotes teacher/toddler 
partnerships and learning through games, by specifically focusing on children’s interests. 


The YMCA believes in integrating children with special needs into its regular programs. This year, 17 
88 children a week participated in our day camps during the summer and 14 children a week attend- 
ed our after-school programs. 


YOUTH SECTOR 


Among the many beneficial activities for youth, a dozen high school girls organized activities in their 
school to build awareness of fair trade practices, the environment, poverty and other topics as part 
of the Hochelaga-Maisonneuve YMCA leadership program. 


Sixteen youth aged 10 to 12 participated in the West Island YMCA Y-Pod program and workshops to 
prepare for high school life. 


More than 300 teens went to the 2007 Youth Festival at the Downtown YMCA. They attended a vari- 
ety show prepared by a hundred or so youth from YMCA centres and visited 15 information kiosks on topics of 
interest to them. 


THE TIES THAT BIND 


Thirty-five youth from The YMCAs of Québec attended the Youth Leaders’ Camp in Spring 2007 at YMCA 
Kanawana, which provides an ideal opportunity to exchange ideas, learn, get involved and have fun. 


18 


THE TIES THAT BIND 


INTERNATIONAL PROGRAMS 


Under the public commitment of its activities, the YMCA, in collaboration with UQAM, hosted 150 
people at a series of conferences on the realities faced by women around the world. 


Last August, YMCA centres actively participated in the first Quebec Social Forum. Throughout the 
year, they also drew attention to local and global environmental threats and issues. 


With over 200 people in attendance, three times more than in previous years, the 20th anniversary of 
the Peace Medal Awards was a wonderful success! In addition to the two former child soldiers from 
Sierre Leone, six local individuals or groups were honoured. 


In terms of international solidarity activities, The YMCAs of Québec sent a delegation to Ecuador and Nicaragua 
and hosted an Ecuadorian colleague, Helga Serrano, who was a speaker at the conference on the internation- 
al demilitarization movement. Our international training program was recognized at the YMCA International 
Conference in Mexico City. 


WELCOMING NEW ARRIVALS 


Last fall, the YMCA Residence saw a large number of asylum seekers arrive from Haiti, many of 
whom were single mothers. The Covered Garden community program quickly deployed strategies to 
deal with the situation: adaptation of the programming, signage in Creole, recruiting volunteers of 
Haitian origin and the establishment of a new daycare service. The Covered Garden clearly demon- 
strated that it could react to change promptly and efficiently. 


The YMCA Residence welcomed close to 4,700 asylum seekers who stayed for an average of 
27 days. They were primarily from Mexico, Haiti, Colombia, Burundi and Congo. 


EDUCATION 


In addition to its language camp offering French courses to youth for the first time ever, the 
International Language School launched its all-new immersion program. “The Language Cruise” 
was designed for participants to learn English in a context of travel and discovery. Guided by the 
educational advisor of the YMCA’s English Department, students sailed up the St. Lawrence River to 
the Magdalen Islands. Talk about un voyage magnifique! 


MANAGEMENT RESOURCE 
CENTRE FOR EASTERN CANADA 


The Management Resource Centre for Eastern Canada located in Halifax provided support services to the 
14 YMCA and YMCA-YWCA associations in Eastern Canada. The role of the Management Resource Centre is 
primarily to respond to requests for services, encourage training and personal development, offer counselling 
services during crises, etc. 


The YMCAs of Québec play a leadership role with these associations, especially by sharing their expertise in 
strategic planning and development. 


Over the past few months, the Centre implemented Accpacc and Class management information systems, 
established an international partnership with the YMCA of Honduras, and worked on asset development and 
investment projects with the Cape Breton and Yarmouth YMCAs, among others. 


THE YMCAsS oF ouésBeEc 


INNOVATION, RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT FUND 


In 2003-04, the YMCA of Greater Montreal created a fund to increase the reach of its programs 
and services. With resources of $100,000 this year, the Innovation, Research and Development 
Fund supported the implementation of new initiatives that maintain the relevance, efficiency, 
and quality of the YMCA’s actions. The projects selected meet strict criteria based on the 
YMCA’s mission and its integration into the community. Projects are also subject to a year-end 
evaluation. 


HERE ARE SOME EXAMPLES OF INITIATIVES FINANCED IN 2007 


Multigenerational Organic Garden Pointe-St-Charles YMCA and YMCA Kanawana $17,100 
Organic gardening to increase awareness of healthy eating habits, organic agriculture, 
and composting among children and adults 


Girlz Club Notre-Dame-de-Grace YMCA $3,300 
A personal development project covering various aspects for girls aged 12 to 19 


Heart and Health Notre-Dame-de-Grace YMCA $4,500 
Specialized cardiovascular training program for adults and seniors 


Environmental Education YMCA Kanawana $6,700 
Environmental education program for campers 


On a Nearby Planet Association $1,240 
A simulation game to help 60 youth become aware of the planet's environmental issues 
and to become involved in sustainable development solutions 


Peace Medals /nternational Programs $4,000 
20th anniversary celebration of this event that pays tribute to community peacemakers 


STIs and HIV/AIDS Education Hochelaga-Maisonneuve YMCA $6,495 
Creation of a board game for youth on the prevention of sexually transmitted 
infections (STIs) and HIV/AIDS
